title: Ezekiel 45:1–8
context: The LORD continues speaking to Ezekiel about the division of the land. When Israel divides the land by lot, a holy portion is to be set apart for the LORD, containing the sanctuary, a region for the priests, a region for the Levites, and a portion for the city that belongs to the whole house of Israel. The prince receives land on either side of the holy portion, so that his princes will no more oppress the people but give the land to the tribes. The fuller allotment appears in 48:8–22. In 45:1 the unit of measure is not stated in the text here, and translations supply cubits or reeds in different places. The concern that rulers not seize the people’s land recalls the warnings of 1 Samuel 8:14 and the story of Naboth (1 Kings 21) and is repeated in 46:18. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat the passage as shared ground about God’s ownership of the land, holiness at the center of the community, and justice from rulers.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Moreover, when you divide by lot the land for inheritance, you shall offer an offering to the LORD, a holy portion of the land. The length shall be the length of twenty-five thousand reeds, and the width shall be ten thousand. It shall be holy in all its border all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a holy portion of the land offered to the LORD when the land is divided. God receives the first and central place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s ownership of the land expressed in the holy portion. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s ordered picture of the land.

verses.text: Of this there shall be a five hundred by five hundred square for the holy place, and fifty cubits for its pasture lands all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a square set apart for the holy place with open land around it. The sanctuary is protected by space.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see symmetry and order expressing holiness. Readers in both traditions commonly read the measurement within the vision’s larger meaning of ordered holiness.

verses.text: Of this measure you shall measure a length of twenty-five thousand, and a width of ten thousand. In it shall be the sanctuary, which is most holy.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sanctuary, most holy, within the measured portion. God’s presence is at the center of the whole land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the most holy place at the heart of the land. Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God dwelling at the center of his people’s life.

verses.text: It is a holy portion of the land; it shall be for the priests, the ministers of the sanctuary, who come near to minister to the LORD. It shall be a place for their houses and a holy place for the sanctuary.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the holy portion given to the priests for their houses and the sanctuary. Those who serve live near God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see provision for the priests within the holy area. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s careful ordering of the land.

verses.text: Twenty-five thousand cubits in length and ten thousand in width shall be for the Levites, the ministers of the house, as a possession for themselves, for twenty rooms.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see land given to the Levites as a possession, for their dwellings. They too have a secure place near the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites receiving a portion alongside the priests. Both traditions commonly read the verse within the vision’s arrangement, without pressing the details.

verses.text: “ ‘ “You shall appoint the possession of the city five thousand cubits wide and twenty-five thousand long, side by side with the offering of the holy portion. It shall be for the whole house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the city’s possession belonging to the whole house of Israel. The city is shared by all the tribes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the city as common ground for the whole people. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of unity in the restored community.

verses.text: “ ‘ “What is for the prince shall be on the one side and on the other side of the holy allotment and of the possession of the city, in front of the holy allotment and in front of the possession of the city, on the west side westward, and on the east side eastward, and in length corresponding to one of the portions, from the west border to the east border.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prince’s land on either side of the holy portion and the city. His place is defined and bounded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prince’s portion fixed so that he need not seize others’ land. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s concern for justice.

verses.text: In the land it shall be to him for a possession in Israel. My princes shall no more oppress my people, but they shall give the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying his princes will no more oppress his people but give the land to the tribes. Justice replaces exploitation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of the warnings in 1 Samuel 8:14 and a promise repeated in 46:18. Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about just rulers.
